questions.topic: Trainee may perform nondiscretionary work but not accept a telephone prescription
questions.trigger: A licensed technician trainee is working beside a pharmacist. A prescriber calls to give a new noncontrolled Schedule VI prescription. The trainee is accurate at data entry and has already completed 500 hours of experience but has not become a licensed technician. What may the trainee do?
questions.legal_decision: Trainee status prohibits taking telephone prescriptions even under direct supervision; authorized nondiscretionary assistance is distinct.
questions.critical_exception: Completed hours do not convert the trainee license into another credential.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A licensed certified technician with pharmacist approval may receive a new telephone prescription.
questions.stem: A licensed technician trainee is working beside a pharmacist. A prescriber calls to give a new noncontrolled Schedule VI prescription. The trainee is accurate at data entry and has already completed 500 hours of experience but has not become a licensed technician. What may the trainee do?

choices.text: Accept the call if the pharmacist listens on an extension.
choices.why: Incorrect. Direct supervision does not remove the prohibition on taking prescriptions by phone.

choices.text: Refer the prescriber to an authorized recipient, then perform delegated data entry under supervision.
choices.why: Correct. The trainee may assist with authorized technical duties, but may not take the telephone prescription.

choices.text: Take the call because Schedule VI is not federally scheduled.
choices.why: Incorrect. The restriction applies to telephone prescriptions without a Schedule VI exception.

choices.text: Take the call after recording the completed experience hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. Experience does not independently change the worker's license or scope.

choices.text: Take the call and authorize the final dispensing validation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither receiving the call nor final dispensing validation is authorized for the trainee.

critical_error_options.rationale: Direct supervision does not remove the prohibition on taking prescriptions by phone.
Neither receiving the call nor final dispensing validation is authorized for the trainee.

questions.topic: New prescription pickup during a sole pharmacist's on-premises break
questions.trigger: A sole pharmacist is taking a 20-minute break on the pharmacy premises. The pharmacy remains secure. A patient arrives for a new prescription that was prepared, visually checked and reviewed for drug utilization by the pharmacist before the break. Which actions are consistent with the temporary-absence rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: A previously prepared, checked and DUR-reviewed new prescription may be picked up with a transaction log including phone number and pharmacist follow-up.
questions.critical_exception: The exception is conditional and does not permit unchecked prescriptions to leave.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist had not completed visual checking and DUR, the new prescription could not be released under this exception.
questions.stem: A sole pharmacist is taking a 20-minute break on the pharmacy premises. The pharmacy remains secure. A patient arrives for a new prescription that was prepared, visually checked and reviewed for drug utilization by the pharmacist before the break. Which actions are consistent with the temporary-absence rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Record the patient's phone number in the required pickup transaction log.
choices.why: Correct. The exception requires a transaction log that includes the patient's telephone number.

choices.text: Allow a technician to supply the professional counseling instead of the pharmacist's follow-up.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technical staff cannot replace the pharmacist's required follow-up.

choices.text: After returning, the pharmacist calls within a reasonable time to address appropriate counseling.
choices.why: Correct. The returning pharmacist must follow up with the patient regarding pertinent counseling.

choices.text: Release another new prescription that has not yet been visually checked.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception requires the pharmacist's check and DUR before release.

choices.text: Omit the log because the patient has used the pharmacy for years.
choices.why: Incorrect. An established relationship does not waive the log for this new prescription.

critical_error_options.rationale: The exception requires the pharmacist's check and DUR before release.

questions.topic: Verification of a new employee's current license at commencement
questions.trigger: A chain hires a technician who shows a national certification card and says the Massachusetts license is active. The manager plans to schedule the technician before confirming the state license. What must the pharmacy do at commencement of employment?
questions.legal_decision: Verify that the individual's license to practice is current.
questions.critical_exception: National certification is not a substitute for current Massachusetts licensure.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy has already verified current state licensure, this specific hiring check is satisfied.
questions.stem: A chain hires a technician who shows a national certification card and says the Massachusetts license is active. The manager plans to schedule the technician before confirming the state license. What must the pharmacy do at commencement of employment?

choices.text: Rely on the national certification card alone.
choices.why: Incorrect. Certification does not establish current state licensure.

choices.text: Wait until the next state renewal cycle to verify the license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verification is required at commencement of employment.

choices.text: Require the technician to apply for a pharmacist license.
choices.why: Incorrect. The applicable credential is the technician's own license.

choices.text: Verify current Massachusetts licensure at commencement of employment.
choices.why: Correct. The pharmacy must verify the current license of the regulated employee.

choices.text: Accept the employee's verbal assurance instead of verifying the license.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires pharmacy verification.

questions.topic: Referral payment from a healthcare facility employee
questions.trigger: A nursing home's discharge coordinator offers to direct residents' prescriptions exclusively to a community pharmacy if the pharmacist pays a fee for each patient referred. No lawful exception is identified. Which response complies with Massachusetts professional standards?
questions.legal_decision: Refuse remuneration tied to referrals from facility personnel.
questions.critical_exception: The payment is conditioned on generating pharmacy business; ordinary compensation for unrelated lawful services is not the stated arrangement.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Without a referral-linked payment, this particular prohibition would not by itself decide a separate arrangement.
questions.stem: A nursing home's discharge coordinator offers to direct residents' prescriptions exclusively to a community pharmacy if the pharmacist pays a fee for each patient referred. No lawful exception is identified. Which response complies with Massachusetts professional standards?

choices.text: Decline the arrangement because the fee is tied to referrals.
choices.why: Correct. The rule prohibits remuneration to or from covered healthcare facility personnel in return for referrals or generated business.

choices.text: Pay the coordinator only for patients with commercial insurance.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule does not make a commercial-insurance exception.

choices.text: Pay the fee in gift cards rather than cash.
choices.why: Incorrect. Items of value are also covered.

choices.text: Pay the fee only after the first prescription is filled.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing timing does not remove the referral link.

choices.text: Accept the arrangement if the coordinator promises not to disclose it.
choices.why: Incorrect. Secrecy does not make referral remuneration lawful.

critical_error_options.rationale: The rule does not make a commercial-insurance exception.
Items of value are also covered.
Changing timing does not remove the referral link.
Secrecy does not make referral remuneration lawful.

questions.topic: Voluntarily expired pharmacist license beyond one renewal cycle
questions.trigger: A pharmacist's Massachusetts license expired December 31, 2022 because the pharmacist stopped practicing in the Commonwealth. In November 2026 the pharmacist wishes to resume practice. The license was never disciplined. Which statements apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Reactivation conditions include passing MPJE and meeting Board conditions; practice before renewal is unlicensed.
questions.critical_exception: This is non-disciplinary expiration, not reinstatement following suspension.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If expiration were only 30 days, the more-than-two-year MPJE requirement would not apply.
questions.stem: A pharmacist's Massachusetts license expired December 31, 2022 because the pharmacist stopped practicing in the Commonwealth. In November 2026 the pharmacist wishes to resume practice. The license was never disciplined. Which statements apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacist may resume dispensing upon submitting an application.
choices.why: Incorrect. A pending application does not restore authority to practice.

choices.text: Passing the MPJE is a prerequisite under the more-than-two-year rule.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly requires it for nondisciplinary expiration of this duration.

choices.text: The pharmacist must meet the Board's other reactivation conditions.
choices.why: Correct. Passing the exam alone does not complete reactivation.

choices.text: The Board must treat this expiration as disciplinary revocation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stated expiration was not imposed as discipline.

choices.text: A current out-of-state license automatically renews the Massachusetts license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Another state's license does not reactivate the Massachusetts credential.

critical_error_options.rationale: A pending application does not restore authority to practice.

questions.topic: Personal email and phone changes on the licensing profile
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts licensed pharmacy technician changes both telephone number and personal email address but not mailing address. The technician does not change employers. What is required for the Board licensing profile?
questions.legal_decision: Update the online licensing profile within 14 calendar days of the change.
questions.critical_exception: The reporting duty applies to each listed personal contact field, even without a move.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If none of the listed personal contact fields changed, this event would not trigger an update.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts licensed pharmacy technician changes both telephone number and personal email address but not mailing address. The technician does not change employers. What is required for the Board licensing profile?

choices.text: Update the profile within 30 business days.
choices.why: Incorrect. The period is 14 calendar days.

choices.text: Wait until the next license renewal.
choices.why: Incorrect. The obligation is triggered by the contact change.

choices.text: Notify only the pharmacy employer.
choices.why: Incorrect. Employer notification does not update the DPH licensing profile.

choices.text: Update only if the mailing address also changes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Phone and email changes independently trigger the requirement.

choices.text: Update both changed fields within 14 calendar days.
choices.why: Correct. The rule expressly includes telephone and email information.

questions.topic: Out-of-state Schedule II nonnarcotic prescription presented after five-day window
questions.trigger: A prescriber who is licensed and DEA-registered in Illinois, but not authorized to prescribe in Massachusetts, issues a methylphenidate prescription on November 4. A Massachusetts retail pharmacist receives it on November 11 and verifies its authenticity. No special exception applies. Which statement is correct?
questions.legal_decision: Do not fill under the out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II pathway when issued more than five days earlier.
questions.critical_exception: The ordinary 30-day Massachusetts Schedule II rule does not extend this specific interstate authorization.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If received within the five-day window and verified, the interstate pathway could apply.
questions.stem: A prescriber who is licensed and DEA-registered in Illinois, but not authorized to prescribe in Massachusetts, issues a methylphenidate prescription on November 4. A Massachusetts retail pharmacist receives it on November 11 and verifies its authenticity. No special exception applies. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Fill because methylphenidate is not a narcotic.
choices.why: Incorrect. Nonnarcotic status permits the interstate pathway but does not eliminate its five-day limit.

choices.text: Fill because verification replaces the time limit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verification and timeliness are separate conditions.

choices.text: Do not fill this prescription; obtain a new lawful prescription if appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Seven days have elapsed, beyond the special five-day authorization.

choices.text: Fill because all Schedule II prescriptions are valid for 30 days regardless of origin.
choices.why: Incorrect. The specific interstate rule is more restrictive.

choices.text: Fill only half now and the remainder later to satisfy the time rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. A partial fill does not restore authority to fill the original prescription.

critical_error_options.rationale: Nonnarcotic status permits the interstate pathway but does not eliminate its five-day limit.
Verification and timeliness are separate conditions.
The specific interstate rule is more restrictive.
A partial fill does not restore authority to fill the original prescription.

questions.topic: Out-of-state oral Schedule IV prescription and follow-up request
questions.trigger: A Vermont practitioner authorized there and federally registered sends an otherwise lawful oral Schedule IV prescription to a Massachusetts pharmacist. Assume a valid electronic-prescribing exception applies and the prescription was issued today. Which actions are required under the Massachusetts out-of-state prescription rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Verify authenticity/validity and record the request for a written follow-up within seven days or shorter federal limit.
questions.critical_exception: An authorized oral transmission and successful verification do not waive the special follow-up request.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the order were from a Massachusetts-authorized practitioner, §18(c)'s interstate-specific provision would not govern.
questions.stem: A Vermont practitioner authorized there and federally registered sends an otherwise lawful oral Schedule IV prescription to a Massachusetts pharmacist. Assume a valid electronic-prescribing exception applies and the prescription was issued today. Which actions are required under the Massachusetts out-of-state prescription rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Verify the prescription by telephone or another appropriate means.
choices.why: Correct. The statute requires verification for interstate Schedule III–V prescriptions.

choices.text: Require a new DEA registration solely because the practitioner lives in Vermont.
choices.why: Incorrect. A practitioner meeting the stated out-of-state requirements need not obtain a separate registration merely to use this pathway.

choices.text: Record that the pharmacist requested the practitioner to send a written prescription within seven days or the shorter applicable federal period.
choices.why: Correct. This is the express requirement for oral interstate Schedule III–V orders.

choices.text: Dispense if authenticity cannot be established but the patient has an insurance card.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute prohibits dispensing if the required verification cannot be obtained.

choices.text: Treat the prescription as Schedule II because it crossed a state line.
choices.why: Incorrect. Origin does not alter the controlled-substance schedule.

critical_error_options.rationale: The statute prohibits dispensing if the required verification cannot be obtained.

questions.topic: Institutional DEA registration does not cover unrelated private practice
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital authorizes a resident to prescribe under the hospital's DEA registration and assigns an internal suffix. On a weekend the resident sees a private patient independently outside the resident's hospital employment. The resident has no individual DEA registration and no other applicable exemption. Which conclusion follows?
questions.legal_decision: The institutional registration exemption applies only within the authorized scope of institutional employment.
questions.critical_exception: The suffix identifies the hospital-authorized practitioner but is not a general independent prescribing credential.
questions.counterfactual_flip: For a patient treated in the usual authorized hospital employment, institutional registration could be sufficient if all conditions are met.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital authorizes a resident to prescribe under the hospital's DEA registration and assigns an internal suffix. On a weekend the resident sees a private patient independently outside the resident's hospital employment. The resident has no individual DEA registration and no other applicable exemption. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: The suffix authorizes private controlled-substance prescribing nationwide.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exemption is restricted to the hospital or institutional employment.

choices.text: The hospital registration alone suffices if the resident is a physician.
choices.why: Incorrect. Professional licensure does not eliminate federal registration conditions.

choices.text: The resident can prescribe privately if a pharmacist verifies the suffix.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verification cannot expand the scope of institutional authorization.

choices.text: The resident cannot rely on the hospital exemption for this independent encounter.
choices.why: Correct. The private encounter falls outside the scope of hospital employment.

choices.text: The resident can issue only one private Schedule II prescription per day using the hospital number.
choices.why: Incorrect. No such numerical exception exists.

critical_error_options.rationale: The exemption is restricted to the hospital or institutional employment.
Professional licensure does not eliminate federal registration conditions.
Verification cannot expand the scope of institutional authorization.
No such numerical exception exists.

questions.topic: Prescription cannot replenish general controlled office stock
questions.trigger: A physician asks a pharmacy to fill a prescription for 100 lorazepam tablets written in the physician's own name. The physician explains that the tablets will be kept as general office stock for future patients, not for treatment of the physician or an identified patient. How should the pharmacist respond?
questions.legal_decision: Decline to fill as a patient prescription; use lawful distribution channels for authorized stock acquisition.
questions.critical_exception: Federal law distinguishes patient prescriptions from stock supply.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A legitimate patient-specific prescription would be assessed under the ordinary prescription validity rules.
questions.stem: A physician asks a pharmacy to fill a prescription for 100 lorazepam tablets written in the physician's own name. The physician explains that the tablets will be kept as general office stock for future patients, not for treatment of the physician or an identified patient. How should the pharmacist respond?

choices.text: Fill if the quantity is less than a typical wholesale package.
choices.why: Incorrect. Quantity does not change the office-stock purpose.

choices.text: Fill because a physician may possess controlled substances.
choices.why: Incorrect. Possession authority is distinct from issuing a patient prescription for general stock.

choices.text: Decline to use a prescription for general office stock and direct the practitioner to lawful acquisition channels.
choices.why: Correct. A controlled prescription may not be issued to supply general dispensing stock.

choices.text: Record the physician as the ultimate user even though no personal treatment is intended.
choices.why: Incorrect. That would misrepresent the stated purpose.

choices.text: Dispense because lorazepam is below Schedule II.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal stock restriction applies to controlled prescriptions generally.

critical_error_options.rationale: Quantity does not change the office-stock purpose.
Possession authority is distinct from issuing a patient prescription for general stock.
That would misrepresent the stated purpose.
The federal stock restriction applies to controlled prescriptions generally.

questions.topic: Tapentadol and tramadol scheduling distinction
questions.trigger: Which classification of tapentadol and tramadol is correct for federal and Massachusetts scheduling of ordinary single-ingredient prescription products?
questions.legal_decision: Tapentadol is Schedule II; tramadol is Schedule IV.
questions.critical_exception: Drug class similarity does not establish the same controlled schedule.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Changing the drug substance changes the applicable schedule, not merely the brand name.
questions.stem: Which classification of tapentadol and tramadol is correct for federal and Massachusetts scheduling of ordinary single-ingredient prescription products?

choices.text: Both are Schedule II.
choices.why: Incorrect. Tramadol is Schedule IV.

choices.text: Tapentadol is Schedule IV and tramadol is Schedule II.
choices.why: Incorrect. The classifications are reversed.

choices.text: Both are Schedule IV.
choices.why: Incorrect. Tapentadol is Schedule II.

choices.text: Tapentadol is Schedule II and tramadol is Schedule IV.
choices.why: Correct. The two drugs are expressly listed in those federal schedules, adopted in Massachusetts.

choices.text: Tapentadol is Schedule VI and tramadol is Schedule V.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither stated classification is correct.

questions.topic: Vaccine preparation and clinical selection by different personnel
questions.trigger: A licensed certified technician has completed all required immunization training and has current CPR. An eligible adult requests a routine vaccine under a valid standing order. The supervising immunizing pharmacist asks the technician to independently evaluate contraindications, select the vaccine and counsel the patient before administering it. Which action is permitted?
questions.legal_decision: Technician may physically prepare and administer after pharmacist counseling and vaccine selection, under required supervision.
questions.critical_exception: Vaccination qualification does not confer independent clinical decision-making authority.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a qualified pharmacist performs the selection and counseling, the trained technician may perform the authorized physical tasks.
questions.stem: A licensed certified technician has completed all required immunization training and has current CPR. An eligible adult requests a routine vaccine under a valid standing order. The supervising immunizing pharmacist asks the technician to independently evaluate contraindications, select the vaccine and counsel the patient before administering it. Which action is permitted?

choices.text: Allow the technician to select the vaccine and counsel without pharmacist involvement.
choices.why: Incorrect. The technician's vaccine scope is limited to specified physical tasks.

choices.text: Have the pharmacist counsel and select the vaccine, then permit supervised technician preparation and administration.
choices.why: Correct. This preserves the clinical/technical division established by the policy.

choices.text: Permit independent technician selection if the patient has been vaccinated previously.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prior vaccination does not expand technician scope.

choices.text: Delegate the clinical judgment to the technician if the pharmacy is busy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Workload does not waive the pharmacist's responsibility.

choices.text: Prohibit the technician from physically administering any vaccine under any circumstances.
choices.why: Incorrect. Qualified technicians are permitted to administer under the stated conditions.

critical_error_options.rationale: The technician's vaccine scope is limited to specified physical tasks.
Prior vaccination does not expand technician scope.
Workload does not waive the pharmacist's responsibility.

questions.topic: VAERS mandatory events and MIIS reporting
questions.trigger: A pharmacist administers a routine vaccine under a valid order. The patient subsequently experiences an event that the manufacturer lists as a contraindication to further doses. The event occurs outside the interval for a different event listed in the VAERS table. Which statements apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Report the manufacturer-listed contraindication to VAERS and report vaccination information to MIIS.
questions.critical_exception: The two mandatory VAERS criteria are alternatives, not cumulative; MIIS is separate.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an event met neither mandatory category, this policy would not mandate VAERS reporting solely under those categories.
questions.stem: A pharmacist administers a routine vaccine under a valid order. The patient subsequently experiences an event that the manufacturer lists as a contraindication to further doses. The event occurs outside the interval for a different event listed in the VAERS table. Which statements apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Submit the required VAERS report because the manufacturer lists the event as a contraindication to further doses.
choices.why: Correct. This is an independent mandatory reporting category.

choices.text: Skip VAERS because the event is outside the interval for a different table event.
choices.why: Incorrect. That does not defeat the separate manufacturer criterion.

choices.text: Ensure the vaccination information is reported to MIIS.
choices.why: Correct. Reporting administration to MIIS is a distinct obligation.

choices.text: Use MIIS instead of VAERS for the adverse-event report.
choices.why: Incorrect. The systems serve different functions and one does not replace the other.

choices.text: Report only if a lawsuit is filed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Litigation is not a precondition for mandatory reporting.

critical_error_options.rationale: That does not defeat the separate manufacturer criterion.
The systems serve different functions and one does not replace the other.

questions.topic: Patient counseling tailored to relevant missed-dose and monitoring instructions
questions.trigger: A patient accepts counseling for a newly prescribed medication. The pharmacist determines that self-monitoring and what to do after a missed dose are particularly important for safe use. The patient already knows the medication's name and strength. Which approach complies with Massachusetts counseling standards?
questions.legal_decision: Provide counseling using professional judgment about information needed for proper use, including the relevant monitoring and missed-dose actions.
questions.critical_exception: Counseling is individualized rather than limited to reading a label.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a topic is not relevant in the pharmacist's judgment, the illustrative list is not a mandatory identical script for every patient.
questions.stem: A patient accepts counseling for a newly prescribed medication. The pharmacist determines that self-monitoring and what to do after a missed dose are particularly important for safe use. The patient already knows the medication's name and strength. Which approach complies with Massachusetts counseling standards?

choices.text: Ask a technician to make the independent clinical counseling decisions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Counseling is reserved to pharmacists or pharmacy interns.

choices.text: Only repeat the name and strength because the written label is complete.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacist identified additional information necessary for proper use.

choices.text: Explain the pertinent monitoring and missed-dose instructions as part of individualized counseling.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly includes these topics when relevant to understanding proper use.

choices.text: Provide no counseling because the patient can read the label.
choices.why: Incorrect. The patient accepted counseling for new therapy.

choices.text: Read every possible adverse effect regardless of relevance and omit missed-dose instructions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule calls for clinically relevant information based on professional judgment.

critical_error_options.rationale: Counseling is reserved to pharmacists or pharmacy interns.
The patient accepted counseling for new therapy.

questions.topic: Return of pharmacy-dispensed product suspected contaminated
questions.trigger: A patient returns a bottle dispensed by the pharmacy two days earlier. The seal appears intact, but the pharmacist reasonably suspects the contents are contaminated. Another patient brings back an intact, properly dispensed, nondefective bottle solely because treatment was discontinued. No special return program applies. Which actions follow the general rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Accept the suspected contaminated medication; quarantine and properly dispose rather than return to inventory. Acceptance of the other product is not required by this rule.
questions.critical_exception: An intact seal does not override the suspected-defect rule or authorize redispensing.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A medication properly dispensed and not defective at dispensing is not subject to mandatory acceptance solely for changed treatment.
questions.stem: A patient returns a bottle dispensed by the pharmacy two days earlier. The seal appears intact, but the pharmacist reasonably suspects the contents are contaminated. Another patient brings back an intact, properly dispensed, nondefective bottle solely because treatment was discontinued. No special return program applies. Which actions follow the general rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Accept the suspected contaminated bottle.
choices.why: Correct. The pharmacy must accept its own previously dispensed medication when suspected defective or contaminated.

choices.text: Return that bottle to saleable inventory if the seal looks intact.
choices.why: Incorrect. Accepted suspected defective medication cannot be returned to inventory.

choices.text: Quarantine and properly dispose of the accepted suspect medication.
choices.why: Correct. The rule specifies quarantine and proper disposal.

choices.text: The pharmacy is required by this rule to accept the other properly dispensed nondefective bottle.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule does not impose mandatory acceptance in that case.

choices.text: Dispense the suspect medication to another patient after a visual inspection.
choices.why: Incorrect. A visual inspection does not authorize return to inventory or redispensing.

critical_error_options.rationale: Accepted suspected defective medication cannot be returned to inventory.
A visual inspection does not authorize return to inventory or redispensing.

questions.topic: HIPAA disclosure when competent patient expressly objects
questions.trigger: A competent adult is present at the pharmacy with a friend. The patient explicitly tells the pharmacist not to disclose any prescription information to the friend. The friend later asks the pharmacist what medication the patient received. No other permitted disclosure basis or legal requirement applies. How should the pharmacist respond?
questions.legal_decision: Honor the patient's express objection and do not disclose prescription information to the friend.
questions.critical_exception: The informal involvement-in-care pathway cannot override an available competent patient's objection.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the patient agreed or did not object after a meaningful opportunity, directly relevant information could be disclosed.
questions.stem: A competent adult is present at the pharmacy with a friend. The patient explicitly tells the pharmacist not to disclose any prescription information to the friend. The friend later asks the pharmacist what medication the patient received. No other permitted disclosure basis or legal requirement applies. How should the pharmacist respond?

choices.text: Disclose only the name of the drug because no dose is requested.
choices.why: Incorrect. Even the drug name is protected information subject to the objection.

choices.text: Disclose if the friend says they drove the patient to the pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The express objection defeats inference of consent under this pathway.

choices.text: Disclose if the friend offers to pay for the medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payment involvement alone does not override the patient's objection.

choices.text: Decline to disclose the prescription information.
choices.why: Correct. The competent patient has expressly objected and no other basis applies.

choices.text: Provide the information after the patient leaves the counter.
choices.why: Incorrect. The known objection does not disappear when the patient steps away.

critical_error_options.rationale: Even the drug name is protected information subject to the objection.
The express objection defeats inference of consent under this pathway.
Payment involvement alone does not override the patient's objection.
The known objection does not disappear when the patient steps away.

questions.topic: FDA REMS dispensing authorization not satisfied
questions.trigger: A patient presents a valid prescription for a drug subject to an FDA-required REMS that specifically requires the dispensing pharmacy to obtain a program authorization before each dispense. The prescription and insurance claim are valid, but the required authorization has not been obtained. Which action is appropriate?
questions.legal_decision: Withhold dispensing until the applicable REMS condition is met.
questions.critical_exception: Ordinary prescription and payment validation do not override a product-specific REMS restriction.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If all applicable REMS dispensing conditions are met, this particular restriction no longer blocks dispensing.
questions.stem: A patient presents a valid prescription for a drug subject to an FDA-required REMS that specifically requires the dispensing pharmacy to obtain a program authorization before each dispense. The prescription and insurance claim are valid, but the required authorization has not been obtained. Which action is appropriate?

choices.text: Dispense now and request program authorization afterward.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stated REMS condition must be satisfied before dispensing.

choices.text: Dispense a one-day supply without authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. No partial-supply exception is stated.

choices.text: Use a prescriber signature as a substitute for REMS authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescription validity does not establish REMS compliance.

choices.text: Delay dispensing until the specific REMS requirement has been satisfied.
choices.why: Correct. Massachusetts requires compliance with all FDA-required REMS dispensing restrictions.

choices.text: Ask the patient to sign a waiver releasing the pharmacy from the REMS.
choices.why: Incorrect. A patient waiver cannot cancel a mandatory REMS condition.

critical_error_options.rationale: The stated REMS condition must be satisfied before dispensing.
No partial-supply exception is stated.
Prescription validity does not establish REMS compliance.
A patient waiver cannot cancel a mandatory REMS condition.

questions.topic: Controlled prescription positive identification hardship exception
questions.trigger: An adult comes to collect an otherwise valid Schedule IV prescription without a government-issued ID. The pharmacist has reason to believe failure to dispense would create a serious hardship. The patient can write and sign their identifying information. No Commissioner waiver otherwise applies. Which actions are required to use the Massachusetts hardship exception? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Document the serious hardship reason and obtain the patient's printed name, address and signature on the permitted record.
questions.critical_exception: Lack of identification alone is not the exception; both conditions must be satisfied.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If there were no serious hardship and no other exception, the normal customer identifier requirement would apply.
questions.stem: An adult comes to collect an otherwise valid Schedule IV prescription without a government-issued ID. The pharmacist has reason to believe failure to dispense would create a serious hardship. The patient can write and sign their identifying information. No Commissioner waiver otherwise applies. Which actions are required to use the Massachusetts hardship exception? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Document why not dispensing would create serious hardship.
choices.why: Correct. The hardship finding must be documented.

choices.text: Obtain the patient's printed name and address and signature on the prescription reverse or permitted log.
choices.why: Correct. This is the second required element of the exception.

choices.text: Record an invented government ID number so the system accepts the claim.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception does not authorize falsifying identification data.

choices.text: Omit all documentation because the pharmacist recognizes the patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Recognition does not satisfy the stated exception requirements.

choices.text: Require a new prescription solely because the patient lacks an ID.
choices.why: Incorrect. A new prescription is not a condition of the hardship exception.

critical_error_options.rationale: The exception does not authorize falsifying identification data.
Recognition does not satisfy the stated exception requirements.

questions.topic: Initial EPCS transfer corrupted by intermediary conversion
questions.trigger: At the patient's request, a retail pharmacy attempts a first transfer of an unfilled original electronic Schedule III prescription to a Massachusetts retail pharmacy. The intermediary converts it to a fax and truncates the prescriber's address. The receiver can independently locate the address. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense from the altered/converted transfer; authorized initial EPCS transfer must remain electronic with required contents intact.
questions.critical_exception: The one-time patient-requested transfer authority does not permit conversion or alteration.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If transmitted electronically without alteration, directly between pharmacists with required documentation and other conditions met, a first transfer could be lawful.
questions.stem: At the patient's request, a retail pharmacy attempts a first transfer of an unfilled original electronic Schedule III prescription to a Massachusetts retail pharmacy. The intermediary converts it to a fax and truncates the prescriber's address. The receiver can independently locate the address. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The conversion to fax violates the initial electronic transfer requirements.
choices.why: Correct. The prescription must remain in electronic form during transfer.

choices.text: The receiving pharmacist may dispense after typing the missing address into the fax record.
choices.why: Incorrect. Alteration of required contents invalidates the transfer; manual repair does not cure it.

choices.text: The truncation is independently a reason the transferred prescription is invalid.
choices.why: Correct. The federal rule expressly prohibits alteration or truncation.

choices.text: A patient request waives the electronic-form requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient request is a prerequisite, not a waiver.

choices.text: All remaining refills can be dispensed from the corrupted transfer because it is Schedule III.
choices.why: Incorrect. Refill authority does not cure the invalid initial transfer.

critical_error_options.rationale: Alteration of required contents invalidates the transfer; manual repair does not cure it.
Refill authority does not cure the invalid initial transfer.

questions.topic: Prospective DUR during computerized pharmacy downtime
questions.trigger: A community pharmacy's software is temporarily offline. Staff can access enough reliable information to perform a manual review and can record dispensing transactions for later entry. Which statements are consistent with Massachusetts practice standards? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: The downtime procedure must provide for appropriate DUR and later recording in the patient's computerized profile.
questions.critical_exception: Technology failure does not waive prospective review or patient-record completion.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Once the system is restored, entries made during downtime must be transferred to the computerized profile.
questions.stem: A community pharmacy's software is temporarily offline. Staff can access enough reliable information to perform a manual review and can record dispensing transactions for later entry. Which statements are consistent with Massachusetts practice standards? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Perform an appropriate prospective DUR using available reliable information before dispensing a new prescription.
choices.why: Correct. Downtime procedures must address appropriate review, and the ordinary DUR obligation remains.

choices.text: Dispense new prescriptions without DUR and perform the first review after restoration.
choices.why: Incorrect. A retrospective review cannot replace the required prospective review.

choices.text: Record prescriptions dispensed during downtime in the patient's computerized profile when the system becomes operational.
choices.why: Correct. The written downtime procedure must address this recording process.

choices.text: Treat every insurer approval as proof that prospective DUR is complete.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payment approval does not constitute the pharmacist's DUR.

choices.text: Discard downtime transaction records once the system restarts without updating patient profiles.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation expressly requires profile reconciliation.

critical_error_options.rationale: A retrospective review cannot replace the required prospective review.
Payment approval does not constitute the pharmacist's DUR.
The regulation expressly requires profile reconciliation.

questions.topic: PMP reporting distinction between inpatient medication order and discharge prescription
questions.trigger: A registered hospital pharmacy dispenses a Schedule IV medication under an order to a currently admitted inpatient. At discharge, the hospital outpatient pharmacy fills a separate reportable Schedule IV prescription for the patient to take home. No other reporting exemption applies. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.legal_decision: Inpatient medication-order dispensing is exempt; the separate outpatient prescription is reportable.
questions.critical_exception: The exemption is tied to dispensing under an inpatient medication order, not the hospital's identity.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If both transactions were medication orders for a current inpatient, the inpatient exemption could apply to both.
questions.stem: A registered hospital pharmacy dispenses a Schedule IV medication under an order to a currently admitted inpatient. At discharge, the hospital outpatient pharmacy fills a separate reportable Schedule IV prescription for the patient to take home. No other reporting exemption applies. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: Report both solely because the hospital holds a registration.
choices.why: Incorrect. The inpatient medication-order exemption expressly applies.

choices.text: Report neither because both transactions occur in a hospital building.
choices.why: Incorrect. The outpatient prescription does not share the inpatient exemption.

choices.text: Report the inpatient order but not the discharge prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. This reverses the rule.

choices.text: Report the separate discharge prescription; the inpatient medication order is exempt.
choices.why: Correct. The decisive distinction is the type of dispensing and inpatient status.

choices.text: Report only if the patient changes hospitals.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing hospitals is not the reporting trigger.

questions.topic: Schedule II shortage partial fill cannot use patient-requested deadline retroactively
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy has only 10 of 30 prescribed Schedule II tablets in stock. The pharmacist documents a shortage-based partial fill today. Neither the patient nor the prescriber requested a patient-requested or prescriber-requested partial fill, and the patient is not terminally ill or in an LTCF. Stock arrives 96 hours after the first partial fill. The original prescription would otherwise remain within its issuance validity period. What is required?
questions.legal_decision: Notify the prescriber if balance not supplied within 72 hours; no further quantity without a new prescription.
questions.critical_exception: Shortage-based partial fill is governed by §1306.13(a), not the different request-based rule.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If remaining stock arrives within 72 hours and prescription remains valid, the balance can be supplied under the shortage rule.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy has only 10 of 30 prescribed Schedule II tablets in stock. The pharmacist documents a shortage-based partial fill today. Neither the patient nor the prescriber requested a patient-requested or prescriber-requested partial fill, and the patient is not terminally ill or in an LTCF. Stock arrives 96 hours after the first partial fill. The original prescription would otherwise remain within its issuance validity period. What is required?

choices.text: Dispense the balance because the prescription is less than 30 days old.
choices.why: Incorrect. The separate 72-hour shortage rule has expired.

choices.text: Treat the original partial fill as patient-requested after the fact without a qualifying request.
choices.why: Incorrect. The request-based pathway was not established in the stated circumstances.

choices.text: Notify the prescriber and require a new prescription before dispensing further quantity.
choices.why: Correct. The federal shortage rule requires notification and prohibits further dispensing without a new prescription after 72 hours.

choices.text: Dispense 10 additional tablets and leave the rest unfilled.
choices.why: Incorrect. Any further quantity after the cutoff requires a new prescription.

choices.text: Refill the original Schedule II prescription for the balance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Schedule II refills are prohibited, and the shortage balance cannot now be supplied.

critical_error_options.rationale: The separate 72-hour shortage rule has expired.
The request-based pathway was not established in the stated circumstances.
Any further quantity after the cutoff requires a new prescription.
Schedule II refills are prohibited, and the shortage balance cannot now be supplied.

questions.topic: Prescriber-specific conventional package request does not carry to another prescription
questions.trigger: A physician directs use of an easy-open container for one oral prescription subject to child-resistant packaging. The patient later presents a different prescription from the same physician with no such direction. The patient has never requested conventional packaging for all medicines. Both drugs are otherwise subject to special packaging. Which response complies with the PPPA?
questions.legal_decision: Use special packaging for the separate prescription unless a valid new prescriber direction or purchaser request applies.
questions.critical_exception: A prescriber direction for one prescription is not a blanket waiver for other prescriptions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A specific patient request applying to all prescriptions could support conventional packaging for the later prescription.
questions.stem: A physician directs use of an easy-open container for one oral prescription subject to child-resistant packaging. The patient later presents a different prescription from the same physician with no such direction. The patient has never requested conventional packaging for all medicines. Both drugs are otherwise subject to special packaging. Which response complies with the PPPA?

choices.text: Use an easy-open container for all future prescriptions from that physician.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prescription-specific direction does not carry over to different prescriptions.

choices.text: Use child-resistant packaging for the new prescription unless an applicable request or direction is obtained.
choices.why: Correct. Neither a qualifying new direction nor a blanket patient request is present.

choices.text: Use conventional packaging because the drugs are prescribed by the same person.
choices.why: Incorrect. The prescriber's identity does not extend the prior direction.

choices.text: Ask the cashier to decide whether the patient probably prefers easy-open packaging.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception depends on the purchaser's request or prescriber's direction, not staff inference.

choices.text: Never use conventional packaging even if the patient specifically requests it.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute permits the purchaser's specific request.

questions.citation: 15 USC 1473(b); CPSC Poison Prevention Packaging Guide, Part 3

critical_error_options.rationale: A prescription-specific direction does not carry over to different prescriptions.
The prescriber's identity does not extend the prior direction.
The exception depends on the purchaser's request or prescriber's direction, not staff inference.

questions.topic: Expired manufacturer stock cannot be dispensed to patient
questions.trigger: While checking a prescription, the pharmacist finds that the manufacturer's expiration date on the stock bottle passed last month. The patient urgently needs the medicine but is not legally authorized to receive expired stock. Which action is permitted?
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense expired stock to the patient; seek an appropriate unexpired supply.
questions.critical_exception: The rule distinguishes ordinary patient dispensing from transfer to an entity legally authorized to receive such products.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the product were in date and otherwise suitable, expiry would no longer prohibit dispensing.
questions.stem: While checking a prescription, the pharmacist finds that the manufacturer's expiration date on the stock bottle passed last month. The patient urgently needs the medicine but is not legally authorized to receive expired stock. Which action is permitted?

choices.text: Dispense the expired medicine with a verbal warning.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient notification does not override the prohibition.

choices.text: Dispense it if the manufacturer bottle is unopened.
choices.why: Incorrect. An intact bottle does not erase the expiration date.

choices.text: Dispense it after the patient signs consent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Consent does not authorize ordinary dispensing of expired stock.

choices.text: Change the expiration date to the date of dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. A pharmacist cannot extend the manufacturer's expiry by relabeling.

choices.text: Do not dispense the expired drug and seek suitable stock.
choices.why: Correct. Ordinary patient dispensing of an expired product is prohibited.

critical_error_options.rationale: Patient notification does not override the prohibition.
An intact bottle does not erase the expiration date.
Consent does not authorize ordinary dispensing of expired stock.
A pharmacist cannot extend the manufacturer's expiry by relabeling.

questions.topic: DEA Form 222 unexecuted forms kept at another location
questions.trigger: A registered pharmacy keeps blank, unexecuted paper DEA Forms 222 in its chain's administrative office rather than at the registered pharmacy address. What condition must be met under the federal rule governing this arrangement?
questions.legal_decision: Unexecuted forms may be kept or executed away from the printed registered location if promptly delivered to that location upon an authorized inspection.
questions.critical_exception: This permission concerns unexecuted forms, not a blanket offsite-record exemption.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If forms cannot be delivered promptly when an authorized inspection occurs, the stated offsite arrangement is not compliant.
questions.stem: A registered pharmacy keeps blank, unexecuted paper DEA Forms 222 in its chain's administrative office rather than at the registered pharmacy address. What condition must be met under the federal rule governing this arrangement?

choices.text: Blank forms must always be stored at the printed registered address with no exception.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal rule expressly permits another location under a condition.

choices.text: An administrative office may permanently refuse access to the forms.
choices.why: Incorrect. The forms must be delivered promptly upon inspection.

choices.text: Only a wholesaler may keep blank forms away from its registered address.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision is not limited to wholesalers.

choices.text: Ensure prompt delivery of all unexecuted forms to the registered location upon an authorized inspection.
choices.why: Correct. This is the explicit condition for offsite retention or execution.

choices.text: Destroy the forms every time an inspector requests them.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires availability, not destruction.

questions.topic: Electronic controlled prescription records on remote servers
questions.trigger: A DEA-registered pharmacy stores its electronic controlled-substance prescription records on a remote server. At the registered location, staff can retrieve, sort and print the records in an understandable format on demand. The application meets Part 1311. Which statements describe the federal requirements? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Remote servers are allowed if records remain readily retrievable and understandable at the registered location; sorting fields are required.
questions.critical_exception: This concerns electronic prescription records, not permission to move required paper Schedule II files.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If records were not readily retrievable at the registered location, offsite electronic storage would fail the requirement.
questions.stem: A DEA-registered pharmacy stores its electronic controlled-substance prescription records on a remote server. At the registered location, staff can retrieve, sort and print the records in an understandable format on demand. The application meets Part 1311. Which statements describe the federal requirements? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Remote server location is not by itself prohibited.
choices.why: Correct. Electronic records may reside on computers at another location.

choices.text: The pharmacy must be able to print or transfer records in a readily understandable format at the registered location.
choices.why: Correct. The rule requires that capability for inspection.

choices.text: The remote server arrangement automatically permits removal of all original Schedule II paper prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Separate requirements apply to paper Schedule II prescriptions.

choices.text: Electronic copies must be sortable by prescriber, patient, dispensed drug and date filled.
choices.why: Correct. These are the listed sorting fields.

choices.text: The pharmacy may deny access because the server is operated by a vendor.
choices.why: Incorrect. The registrant must maintain retrievability at the registered location.

critical_error_options.rationale: The registrant must maintain retrievability at the registered location.

questions.topic: Workplace prescription collection and undelivered medication
questions.trigger: A pharmacy lawfully collects prescriptions from employees at a factory using its authorized agent. The agent returns with patient-specific medications, but one employee is absent and has not designated anyone to receive the medication. The factory supervisor offers to keep it in a locked desk until the employee returns. What should the agent do?
questions.legal_decision: Return the undelivered medication to the pharmacy; workplace collection arrangement requires direct delivery to patient or agent.
questions.critical_exception: A locked workplace storage location does not replace direct delivery.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an actual authorized patient agent were present, direct delivery to that person could satisfy this condition.
questions.stem: A pharmacy lawfully collects prescriptions from employees at a factory using its authorized agent. The agent returns with patient-specific medications, but one employee is absent and has not designated anyone to receive the medication. The factory supervisor offers to keep it in a locked desk until the employee returns. What should the agent do?

choices.text: Leave the medication in the supervisor's locked desk.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule prohibits leaving or storing undelivered medication at the site.

choices.text: Return the medication to the pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. Medication not delivered directly to the patient or patient's agent must be returned.

choices.text: Leave it with any coworker employed at the same factory.
choices.why: Incorrect. Employment at the site does not establish authority to receive another patient's prescription.

choices.text: Leave it at a designated table if the package is sealed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Sealing does not waive direct delivery.

choices.text: Ask the employer to dispense it on the pharmacy's behalf later.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stated arrangement does not authorize the employer to store and dispense undelivered medication.

critical_error_options.rationale: The rule prohibits leaving or storing undelivered medication at the site.
Employment at the site does not establish authority to receive another patient's prescription.
Sealing does not waive direct delivery.
The stated arrangement does not authorize the employer to store and dispense undelivered medication.

questions.topic: Interchangeable biologic substitution when no interoperable EHR access
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist substitutes an FDA-interchangeable biological product for a brand-name biological prescription. No patient-specific written prohibition applies. The pharmacy cannot enter a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record. Which actions are consistent with the Massachusetts biologic substitution statute? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Notify prescriber within reasonable time by permitted alternate method; notify patient or representative in writing; retain substitution record for at least statutory minimum.
questions.critical_exception: Lack of EHR access triggers alternate notification, not a waiver of notice.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a patient-specific written prohibition were present, the substitution itself would not be permitted.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist substitutes an FDA-interchangeable biological product for a brand-name biological prescription. No patient-specific written prohibition applies. The pharmacy cannot enter a notation in the patient's interoperable electronic health record. Which actions are consistent with the Massachusetts biologic substitution statute? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Notify the prescriber within a reasonable time by fax or another permitted alternative.
choices.why: Correct. The statute provides alternate methods when EHR notation is unavailable.

choices.text: Omit notification to the prescriber because the pharmacy lacks EHR access.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute expressly supplies alternate notice methods.

choices.text: Provide written notification of the substitution to the patient or authorized representative.
choices.why: Correct. The patient notification must be written.

choices.text: Retain the substitution record for at least one year from the last profile entry, subject to any longer applicable record rules.
choices.why: Correct. This is the statute's minimum retention provision.

choices.text: Treat verbal patient notice alone as sufficient under §12EE(e).
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute specifies written notification.

questions.topic: Customary simple nonsterile compounding cannot be refused as a blanket policy
questions.trigger: A community pharmacy has all required equipment, trained personnel and materials to prepare a simple nonsterile compound customary to local community needs. It receives an otherwise appropriate lawful prescription. Management directs staff to refuse all such prescriptions solely because ordinary dispensing is more profitable. No extenuating circumstances or Board waiver exist. Which conclusion follows?
questions.legal_decision: A blanket refusal on profitability alone is not consistent with the rule requiring customary simple/moderate nonsterile compounding absent an exception.
questions.critical_exception: Actual extenuating circumstances or a Board waiver can change the obligation; the stem expressly excludes them.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A Board waiver or genuine extenuating circumstance could permit refusal.
questions.stem: A community pharmacy has all required equipment, trained personnel and materials to prepare a simple nonsterile compound customary to local community needs. It receives an otherwise appropriate lawful prescription. Management directs staff to refuse all such prescriptions solely because ordinary dispensing is more profitable. No extenuating circumstances or Board waiver exist. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: The pharmacy may refuse all such prescriptions merely because the margin is low.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation prohibits refusal of customary simple/moderate compounding absent a recognized exception.

choices.text: The pharmacy must compound every complex sterile product as well.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cited obligation is not a universal requirement to perform complex sterile compounding.

choices.text: The pharmacy should comply with the customary simple nonsterile compounding obligation.
choices.why: Correct. The pharmacy has no stated extenuating circumstance or waiver.

choices.text: A referral to another pharmacy automatically waives the obligation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Referral alone is not the specified exception.

choices.text: An internal corporate policy functions as a Board waiver.
choices.why: Incorrect. Internal policy is not a Board-issued waiver.

questions.topic: Ownership transfer requires outgoing notice and incoming application
questions.trigger: A corporate buyer acquires a licensed Massachusetts retail pharmacy through a transaction involving a new legal owner and a new federal employer identification number. The premises and manager of record will remain the same. Which actions are required under the pharmacy ownership-transfer rules? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Outgoing licensee must provide advance notice; incoming licensee must submit a new pharmacy license application; bill of sale and controlled-substance transfer information are required.
questions.critical_exception: Same premises and MOR do not convert a new legal owner into the existing licensee.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If only the operating name changed without ownership transfer, the separate name-change rule would govern.
questions.stem: A corporate buyer acquires a licensed Massachusetts retail pharmacy through a transaction involving a new legal owner and a new federal employer identification number. The premises and manager of record will remain the same. Which actions are required under the pharmacy ownership-transfer rules? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Outgoing licensee notifies the Board at least 14 days before transfer.
choices.why: Correct. The transfer rule imposes this advance notification duty.

choices.text: The incoming owner may simply inherit the existing pharmacy license.
choices.why: Incorrect. A proposed new licensee must apply for its own license.

choices.text: Incoming owner submits its new license application at least 14 days before the transfer.
choices.why: Correct. This is the express minimum advance filing period; earlier filing may be recommended.

choices.text: Submit the required bill of sale and controlled-substance transfer description in support of the application.
choices.why: Correct. Both are listed application materials.

choices.text: No ownership procedure applies if the manager of record remains unchanged.
choices.why: Incorrect. A retained manager does not remove the legal ownership change.

questions.citation: 247 CMR 6.11(1)–(3); Board Pharmacy Application Checklist, Ownership Changes
